prompt:
Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

TEXT_G:
UKIP’s 2005 manifesto argues that Britain’s real government now sits in Brussels and that no other reforms are possible until the UK leaves the EU. The party is not anti-European; it insists the best people to run Britain are the British. Its core aim is an independent, deregulated, free-trading Britain that restores democratic accountability, local control and traditional values of trust, responsibility and national pride.

Independence and timetable
- Repeal the European Communities Act to restore the supremacy of UK law, stop payments to the EU, regain an independent WTO seat and replace EU rules with UK-made laws in a two-year transition. Replace CAP and CFP with British policies and strike bilateral trade and cooperation deals with EU states.

Economy, regulation and trade
- Keep open trade with the EU via Swiss-style agreements; expand global trade with the Commonwealth, NAFTA and Asia; regain leverage at the WTO to press for freer trade.
- Scrap damaging EU-derived regulations, with a presumption to repeal unless retention is overwhelmingly justified, prioritising relief for small firms and ending rules like the Working Time Directive.

Budget and tax
- Redirect UK contributions to the EU to raise state pensions; temporarily raise borrowing (to about a 6% deficit) to fund immediate tax cuts and defence.
- Immediate tax changes: halve council tax for all, scrap the 10% income tax band, raise the inheritance tax threshold to £500,000, and reinstate dividend tax credits to rescue pensions.
- Longer term: simplify and cut taxes—merge National Insurance with income tax, replace VAT with a wholesale sales tax, and consider a low-rate flat tax to spur growth and reduce evasion.

Health, welfare and pensions
- End central micromanagement of the NHS; restore local control, bring back matrons, scrap SHAs, extend GP hours, and let clinicians treat on clinical need not targets. Allow complementary private insurance as in other countries.
- Simplify benefits, reduce means-testing and restore independence from welfare.
- Lift state pensions modestly using EU savings; reinstate dividend tax credits; unfreeze expatriate pensions. Reject mass immigration as a pensions fix.

Education
- Restore school autonomy; scrap SATs; back heads on exclusions; support discipline, sport, trips and teaching of British history and values. Encourage specialist schools with limited selection.
- Expand choice: assisted places, vouchers or tax rebates for private education.
- Review university standards, close weak courses, fully fund strong ones, cancel top-up fees, restore grants and charge EU students full fees.

Law and order, borders and asylum
- Tougher, credible sentencing; more local accountability of police; cut paperwork; defend homeowners; build prisons; resist EU Corpus Juris.
- Aim for near-zero net immigration: a non-discriminatory points system; end automatic EU preference; stricter family reunion; embarkation controls; language/“Britishness” tests; health checks; faster removals; redefine refugee rules. No quotas.

Farming and fishing
- Leave CAP; replace with deficiency payments/minimum prices; curb supermarket power; consider reviving the Milk Marketing Board; cut red tape; reopen local abattoirs; back green/organic methods.
- Leave CFP; reclaim UK waters; rebuild protection fleet; enforce conservation zones and gear rules.

Defence and foreign affairs
- Sovereign defence policy; maintain NATO ties; leave EU defence plans; reverse force cuts; buy British where possible; deploy only in the national interest; keep independent seats in global bodies.

Energy, environment and transport
- Stop wind farm rollout; build new nuclear; develop clean coal and fund fusion research.
- Take back control of environmental law; prioritise recycling; protect countryside; ban GM crop planting until proven safe.
- Invest in roads; set sensible speed limits and target cameras; choose rail structures that work (including reintegration if needed); continue upgrades.

Governance and civil liberties
- Defend the Commons, the Crown, common law and an independent Lords; citizen-initiated referendums at 5% of the electorate; English votes for English laws.
- Scrap English regional assemblies; return business rates and housing transfer duties to councils; cut politically correct bureaucracy.
- Repeal the Human Rights Act; reject the EU Charter; scrap ID cards; repeal the Hunting Act.

Vision
An independent Britain—freer, safer, more prosperous—run by accountable institutions, with smaller government, stronger families, revitalised enterprise and a renewed sense of national purpose.

TEXT_E:
Britain forward, not back. New Labour’s 2005 manifesto applies enduring Labour values to a changing world with one core duty: government must provide opportunity and security for all. It seeks to embed a progressive consensus that rejects the old false choices between wealth creation and social justice, security and liberty, equal rights and protection from crime. The offer is investment plus reform; rights matched by responsibilities; services free to all, personal to each.

Record: macroeconomic stability, record employment, low inflation and mortgage rates; tax credits and a minimum wage that make work pay; real-terms investment transforming schools and the NHS; crime down 30%; poverty reduced for children and pensioners; stronger leadership in Europe; doubled aid and first-in-class action on climate through emissions trading.

Economy: entrench low debt and high employment under strict fiscal rules and a 2% inflation target; no rise in basic or top income tax rates, no VAT on essentials; redirect £21bn efficiencies to the frontline. Build an “opportunity economy” with skills, science (R&D to 2.5% of GDP by 2014), support for manufacturing and SMEs, fair procurement, lighter, smarter regulation, and competitive capital markets. Aim for 80% employment via New Deal, higher minimum wage, incapacity benefit reform, and personalised back-to-work support. Invest over £180bn in transport to 2015, with better rail, potential high-speed links, bus concessions, safety and low-carbon innovation, while exploring fair road pricing. Spread prosperity to every region; strengthen equality at work; back thriving rural economies and environmental stewardship.

Education: personalised learning and parental partnership from early years to HE. More teachers and support staff; primary basics plus arts, sport and languages; every secondary an independent specialist school, with fair admissions, strong discipline, and 200 Academies by 2010; Building Schools for the Future for modern facilities; stretch for the brightest and targeted catch-up. Transform 14–19 with high-quality vocational routes, specialised diplomas, apprenticeships and EMAs; reform FE; expand HE with fair, capped variable fees, bursaries and grants, and a 50% participation aim.

Crime and security: neighbourhood policing teams in every community; firm action on antisocial behaviour and alcohol-related disorder; tackle drugs with compulsory testing and treatment; create the Serious Organised Crime Agency; tougher penalties on guns and knives; cut reoffending with end-to-end offender management; strengthen victims’ rights. Managed migration that benefits Britain: a points-based system favouring skills, secure borders with biometrics and ID cards, faster, fairer asylum. Tackle terrorism with robust laws while upholding liberties.

NHS: free to all, personal to each; no charges for operations. Triple spending by 2008; cut referral-to-treatment waits to 18 weeks; expand capacity via NHS, independent and voluntary providers meeting NHS standards; extend patient choice; shift care to primary and community settings, including new community hospitals; drive cleanliness and clinical governance; focus on prevention—healthier school meals, food labelling, smoke-free workplaces and expanded cessation services.

Older people and families: maintain Pension Credit and universal benefits; build a cross-party pensions settlement that rewards saving; flexible retirement and work beyond 65; individual care budgets. End child poverty in a generation with tax credits, a Child Trust Fund, universal early years, 3,500 Sure Start Children’s Centres, extended schools 8–6, more paid maternity leave and flexible working; boost homeownership and renew social housing with more choice.

International: a leading Britain in a reformed EU; constitutional treaty by referendum; NATO at the core of defence; modern, well-equipped armed forces and a retained independent nuclear deterrent; support for democracy in Iraq and the Middle East; UN, World Bank and IMF reform. Global leadership on climate change (−20% CO2 by 2010, −60% by 2050) and on Africa (0.7% ODA by 2013, debt relief, fairer trade, universal access to AIDS treatment and basic services).

Quality of life and democracy: culture and sport for all (free museums, facilities, Olympic legacy); digital switchover; cleaner neighbourhoods, greener planning, a Marine Act. Devolution deepened; stronger, more accountable local government and neighbourhood powers; complete Lords reform; a Single Equality Act and a new Commission on Equality and Human Rights. The social contract remains clear: we help you; you help yourself; we all move forward together.
